case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the National Bank Act, as amended by Dodd-Frank, preempts a state law requiring banks to pay interest on mortgage escrow-account balances because the state requirement prevents or significantly interferes with a national bank’s exercise of its banking powers under the Barnett Bank preemption standard.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1) (Dodd-Frank Act’s NBA preemption provision, especially § 25b(b)(1)(B) incorporating the Barnett Bank standard); National Bank Act generally (12 U.S.C. § 1 et seq.); related state consumer financial law requiring escrow interest (e.g., New York General Obligations Law § 5-601 as referenced).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Dodd-Frank confirms and tightens the governing preemption inquiry by codifying the Supreme Court’s Barnett Bank standard; under that standard, a state escrow-interest requirement is a generally applicable consumer financial protection law that does not 'prevent or significantly interfere' with a national bank’s exercise of its powers, so it should not be preempted. They also contend that lower courts (and/or the OCC’s approach) have applied an overly broad or categorical preemption analysis inconsistent with Barnett Bank and Dodd-Frank’s framework, which contemplates a careful, context-specific interference analysis rather than automatic displacement of state law.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Bank of America) contends that the state escrow-interest mandate intrudes on and significantly interferes with core federally authorized banking operations (including mortgage lending and escrow administration) and is therefore preempted under the NBA as understood through Barnett Bank and subsequent preemption cases. Respondent also seeks to rely on alternative routes to preemption recognized in Dodd-Frank (including arguments that other federal banking provisions may independently preempt the state law), and maintains that the state law effectively regulates national banks’ federally permitted terms and practices in a way that federal law does not allow states to do.
key_precedents: Barnett Bank of Marion County, N.A. v. Nelson, 517 U.S. 25 (1996)
Sonotone Corp., 442 U.S. 330 (1979) (cited for ordinary meaning/interpretive principles in the excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that an escrow-interest mandate can affect a core servicing term and, in some settings, could rise to “significant interference” under Barnett Bank as incorporated by § 25b(b)(1)(B). But the Second Circuit’s “control” framing risks converting that functional standard into a near-per se rule whenever a State touches pricing or terms, effectively reading “significantly” out of the statute—exactly the overbreadth Dodd-Frank sought to constrain. As Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 25b requires a context-specific, evidence-based showing of practical impairment, not an inference from the mere existence of an added cost or mandated term. The narrow, institutionally legitimate course is therefore to reverse and remand for application of the correct Barnett/§ 25b inquiry, leaving open that a different record could support preemption.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to stress that an escrow-interest mandate directly alters the economics of a federally authorized servicing function, and such a command could amount to “significant interference” in an appropriate case. But the controlling text—§ 25b(b)(1)(B), requiring preemption determinations “in accordance with” Barnett Bank—demands a functional showing that the state law in fact “prevents or significantly interferes,” not merely that it changes terms or imposes costs. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, the Second Circuit’s “control” shorthand risks collapsing “significantly” out of the statute and reintroducing an overbroad displacement rule Congress did not enact. On this record, I do not see the concrete, substantial obstacle Barnett Bank contemplates, so reversal and application of the proper interference inquiry remains the correct course.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s point that § 25b(b)(1)(B) requires a context-specific Barnett Bank inquiry and that a per se “control” label (as Justice Thomas also notes) cannot substitute for the statutory “prevents or significantly interferes” test. But even applying Barnett faithfully, this escrow-interest mandate is not just an incidental compliance cost: it compels the bank to pay a state-set return on escrow balances and thus dictates a material term of mortgage servicing in a way that predictably alters pricing and product structure, which is a significant practical interference with a federally authorized banking power. Justice Kagan’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s characterization of the mandate as a routine consumer-protection baseline understates that it operates as an ongoing, state-imposed transfer affecting the economics of escrow administration across the bank’s portfolio, not merely a one-time disclosure or procedural rule. At most, I could accept a remand to apply Barnett Bank properly, but I do not think the correct application of that standard leaves this law unpreempted on the merits.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press that an escrow-interest mandate can alter the economics of mortgage servicing and, in some cases, could amount to significant interference—but § 25b(b)(1)(B) (codifying Barnett Bank) demands a practical showing of a substantial obstacle, not the Second Circuit’s near-categorical “control” shortcut. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, reading any state regulation of “terms” or increased costs as automatically preempted effectively deletes “significantly” from the statute and revives an overbroad preemption regime Dodd-Frank aimed to narrow. On this record, the law operates as a generally applicable baseline protecting borrower-owned funds rather than a measure that disables escrow administration or meaningfully impairs lending in the McCulloch sense. I would reverse and require the proper evidence-based Barnett/§ 25b inquiry, leaving room for a bank to prove substantial operational impairment in a different case.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that an escrow-interest mandate touches a material servicing term and can affect pricing, so it cannot be waved away as costless; that point matters under Barnett Bank’s practical inquiry. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, § 25b(b)(1)(B) codifies a context-specific “prevents or significantly interferes” test, and the Second Circuit’s categorical “control/terms” framing risks reading “significantly” out of the statute. On this record, the law appears generally applicable and nondiscriminatory and functions as a background rule about borrower-owned funds, so the showing of a substantial obstacle to offering or administering escrow accounts is not established. I therefore stay with reversal (at least to correct the legal standard, and likely on the merits absent stronger evidence of operational impairment).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to stress that a state escrow-interest mandate sets a servicing term and affects pricing, but under the text Congress enacted in § 25b(b)(1)(B) that is not enough: the State must “prevent[] or significantly interfere[]” with the exercise of the national bank power “in accordance with” Barnett Bank. As the Chief Justice notes, the Second Circuit’s “control” shorthand risks collapsing “significantly” into mere cost or term regulation, effectively restoring a broader preemption regime Dodd-Frank curtailed. McCulloch’s anti-“control” principle helps identify impermissible state interference, but it cannot override § 25b’s codified, context-specific standard; on this record there is no concrete showing that paying interest on borrower-owned escrow funds materially impairs the bank’s ability to offer or service mortgages. I therefore remain for the Petitioner and favor reversal with a proper Barnett/§ 25b application rather than a categorical rule either way.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that an escrow-interest mandate can affect a material mortgage-servicing term and thus could, on a fuller showing, rise to “significant interference.” But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 25b(b)(1)(B) codifies a context-specific Barnett Bank inquiry, and the Second Circuit’s “control” shorthand risks turning any state rule that alters costs or terms into automatic preemption, reading “significantly” out of the statute. On this record, the mandate looks like a generally applicable consumer-protection rule imposing an incremental cost rather than a substantial obstacle that prevents or meaningfully impairs the exercise of national-bank powers in the McCulloch/Barnett sense. The appropriate institutional course is to reverse the categorical approach and require an evidence-based application of Barnett/§ 25b, leaving room for preemption in cases where a bank can actually demonstrate significant interference.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that an escrow-interest mandate can affect a material term of mortgage servicing and thus could, in some settings, rise to significant interference. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 25b(b)(1)(B)’s text—“prevents or significantly interferes” “in accordance with” Barnett Bank—demands a context-specific, evidence-based showing of a substantial obstacle, not an inference of preemption from the mere fact that a State has altered costs or terms. McCulloch’s anti-“control” principle helps explain why discriminatory or disabling state regulation is impermissible, but it cannot be converted into the Second Circuit’s categorical “control” shorthand without reading “significantly” out of Congress’s Dodd-Frank codification. On this record, the law appears to impose a generally applicable compliance cost rather than to practically impair the bank’s ability to offer or administer escrow accounts, so preemption is not established (though I agree with Justice Alito that a remand may be appropriate if the lower court applied the wrong legal standard).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that mandated escrow interest dictates a material mortgage-servicing term and can affect pricing—deserves to be taken seriously, because Barnett Bank’s inquiry is ultimately about real-world constraints, not labels. But as the Chief Justice notes, § 25b(b)(1)(B) requires a context-specific showing of “significant” interference “in accordance with” Barnett, and the Second Circuit’s “control” shorthand risks turning any state rule affecting costs or terms into per se preemption. On this record, the escrow-interest requirement looks like a generally applicable baseline governing borrower-owned funds, and—consistent with Justice Kagan’s and Justice Thomas’s emphasis—the bank has not demonstrated a substantial obstacle to offering or administering mortgages, as opposed to an added, manageable cost. McCulloch’s anti-control principle cannot do the work Alito asks here because Congress deliberately narrowed the inquiry in Dodd-Frank to Barnett’s practical, degree-of-interference standard rather than categorical immunity from state consumer-protection rules.

John Roberts.reasoning: Dodd-Frank’s NBA preemption provision, 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B), codifies Barnett Bank’s rule that a state consumer financial law is preempted only if it “prevents or significantly interferes” with a national bank’s exercise of its powers, which calls for a context-specific inquiry rather than a categorical rule. A generally applicable requirement to pay interest on mortgage escrow balances resembles the sort of state consumer-protection regulation that typically coexists with national banking, and on this record it does not appear to rise to the level of significant interference contemplated by Barnett Bank. The Second Circuit’s apparent per se “control” test departs from the narrower standard Congress adopted in § 25b and risks unnecessary displacement of state law, undermining federalism and the dual banking system. A restrained disposition would reverse and remand for application of the proper Barnett Bank/§ 25b standard rather than broad pronouncements about the scope of NBA preemption.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The controlling text is 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B), which expressly incorporates Barnett Bank’s “prevents or significantly interferes” standard, and that language requires a degree-of-interference inquiry rather than a per se rule that any state law “controlling” a banking practice is preempted. Properly applied, a generally applicable escrow-interest requirement does not “prevent” a national bank from exercising its mortgage-lending and escrow-administration powers and, on this record, is at most an incidental cost of doing business—not the kind of substantial obstacle Barnett Bank, 517 U.S. at 33–34, and McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819), treat as preemptive. Because Congress in Dodd-Frank codified that specific standard, courts must apply it as written, and the Second Circuit’s categorical approach improperly departs from the statutory text. The state law should therefore not be preempted absent a showing that it meaningfully and substantially impairs the exercise of the federally conferred power.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B), the question is whether the state escrow-interest mandate “prevents or significantly interferes” with a national bank’s exercise of its federally conferred banking powers, applying the Barnett Bank standard. Requiring a national bank to pay state-prescribed interest on escrow balances directly regulates the terms and costs of a core component of mortgage lending and servicing, and in practical effect meaningfully constrains how the bank structures and prices that federally authorized product. As McCulloch confirms, state laws that operate as a substantial impediment to the exercise of federal instrumentalities’ powers may not be applied, and Barnett Bank likewise preempts state requirements that significantly interfere with federally granted banking authority. Dodd-Frank codified Barnett Bank’s interference inquiry, but it did not convert every state consumer-protection cost mandate into a permissible “incidental” regulation when it materially alters the bank’s mortgage-escrow operations and pricing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Dodd-Frank squarely codifies the Barnett Bank preemption standard for “State consumer financial law[s]” in 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B), requiring a practical, context-specific inquiry into whether the state escrow-interest requirement “prevents or significantly interferes” with a national bank’s powers. A generally applicable escrow-interest mandate functions as a baseline consumer-protection rule governing the handling of borrowers’ funds and does not, on this record, rise to the level of a significant interference with mortgage lending or escrow administration as contemplated by Barnett Bank, 517 U.S. at 33–34. The Second Circuit’s approach—treating the “prevents or significantly interferes” language as effectively irrelevant—conflicts with Congress’s deliberate choice to adopt that specific standard in § 25b(b)(1)(B), and risks overbroad preemption that would strip States of core authority to protect homeowners and other vulnerable consumers. Consistent with Barnett Bank and McCulloch’s limit that federal power does not imply categorical displacement of state law absent a substantial obstacle, the state requirement should not be preempted here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Dodd-Frank’s preemption provision, 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B), directs courts to apply the Barnett Bank standard and thus requires a context-specific inquiry into whether the state escrow-interest requirement “prevents or significantly interferes” with a national bank’s powers, not categorical displacement of generally applicable consumer-financial laws. A state mandate to pay interest on escrow balances functions as a pricing/terms rule of general applicability in mortgage servicing and, without more, is closer to permissible state regulation that increases compliance costs than to the kind of state “control” that amounts to significant interference under Barnett Bank, 517 U.S. at 33–34, 37. Reading § 25b as Congress’s effort to restore a narrower, workable conflict-preemption approach (rather than broad field-like preemption), the bank has not shown that paying interest on funds held for borrowers’ benefit meaningfully impairs the exercise of federally granted lending or escrow-administration powers. Under Barnett Bank and McCulloch’s functional approach to obstacles, the state law can coexist with national bank powers because it regulates the incident of the relationship rather than disabling the power itself.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 25b(b)(1)(B) directs courts to apply the Barnett Bank standard as the governing rule: a state consumer financial law is preempted only if it "prevents or significantly interferes" with a national bank’s exercise of its powers. A generally applicable escrow-interest requirement regulates the incidents of an escrow account but does not, on its face, disable or materially impair a national bank’s federally authorized mortgage lending or servicing in the way Barnett Bank described when state law functioned as a meaningful obstacle to the federal permission. The Second Circuit’s per se approach—treating any state law that “exerts control” over a banking power as preempted—does not track the text Congress chose in § 25b and risks collapsing the “significantly interferes” inquiry into automatic displacement, contrary to Barnett Bank and the separation-of-powers principle that courts must apply the statute as written rather than expand preemption by judicial gloss. To the extent there is ambiguity about the degree of interference here, § 25b’s codification of Barnett Bank demands a concrete, context-specific showing of significant interference, not categorical preemption based on subject-matter labeling.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Dodd-Frank’s 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B) codifies Barnett Bank’s “prevent or significantly interfere” standard and thus rejects a categorical rule that any state law “exerting control” over a banking power is preempted. A generally applicable escrow-interest requirement is a traditional state consumer financial protection measure and, on this record, looks more like an incidental cost of doing business than a prohibition that materially impairs the bank’s federally authorized lending or escrow-administration powers under the National Bank Act. Consistent with Barnett Bank and McCulloch, the inquiry must be practical and context-specific—focused on whether the law meaningfully undermines the exercise of national-bank powers—not an automatic displacement of state law. Because the Second Circuit’s per se approach appears inconsistent with § 25b’s text and Congress’s insistence on a measured, evidence-based interference analysis, I would vote to reverse and hold the state law not preempted on this showing.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B) preempts a state consumer financial law only if it “prevents or significantly interferes” with a national bank’s powers, “in accordance with” Barnett Bank, 517 U.S. 25 (1996), which rejected broad, categorical displacement and instead asked whether the state law meaningfully impairs the federally granted authority. A state requirement to pay interest on mortgage escrow balances regulates the cost of holding borrowers’ funds in connection with mortgage servicing but does not bar escrow administration or mortgage lending, and on this record appears to function as a generally applicable consumer-protection rule rather than a prohibition on banking powers. Consistent with McCulloch’s recognition that States may not “control” federal instrumentalities but may apply nondiscriminatory laws that do not thwart federal ends, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819), the escrow-interest mandate does not rise to the level of significant interference under § 25b’s codified standard. Given Dodd-Frank’s directive for a Barnett Bank–type, context-specific inquiry rather than automatic preemption, the state law is not preempted here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Dodd-Frank’s NBA preemption provision, 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B), expressly incorporates Barnett Bank’s “prevent or significantly interfere” standard, which calls for a context-specific conflict inquiry rather than categorical displacement of generally applicable state consumer-protection rules. A state requirement to pay interest on mortgage escrow balances regulates the handling of borrower funds and functions as a background consumer financial protection law; it does not “control” or meaningfully obstruct a national bank’s core lending power in the way Barnett Bank or McCulloch condemn. Absent a concrete showing that the escrow-interest mandate substantially impairs the bank’s ability to offer mortgages or administer escrow accounts, the practical consequence of preemption would be to remove a traditional state safeguard without the type of significant operational interference Barnett Bank requires. Accordingly, under § 25b’s codified Barnett standard, the state law should not be found preempted on this record.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the National Bank Act, as amended by Dodd-Frank (12 U.S.C. § 25b), preempts a state law requiring national banks to pay interest on mortgage escrow account balances because it “prevents or significantly interferes with” the exercise of national banking powers under the Barnett Bank standard.
case_analysis.legal_provision: National Bank Act preemption as codified/clarified by Dodd-Frank: 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B) (and related preemption framework in § 25b(b)(1)(A)-(C)); state law referenced includes New York General Obligations Law § 5-601 (escrow interest requirement).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Dodd-Frank’s incorporation of the Barnett Bank standard requires a genuine, context-sensitive inquiry into whether the state escrow-interest law meaningfully impairs a national bank’s powers; they contend the Second Circuit applied an overly broad, bank-friendly preemption approach that effectively treats any added cost or operational requirement as “significant interference,” contrary to Barnett and Dodd-Frank’s intent to cabin expansive NBA preemption.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Bank of America) argues that the state escrow-interest mandate is preempted because it materially interferes with national banks’ federally authorized mortgage-lending/escrow operations by dictating how escrow accounts are administered and priced; it also maintains that Dodd-Frank did not materially change the governing NBA preemption standard (it codified Barnett), and under that standard the state requirement imposes a sufficiently significant burden to warrant preemption.
key_precedents: Barnett Bank of Marion County, N.A. v. Nelson, 517 U.S. 25 (1996)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that an escrow-interest mandate is a state-imposed pricing term that “controls” the bank-customer bargain and disrupts national uniformity—has force under McCulloch’s anti-burden principle, but § 25b(b)(1)(B) requires more than identifying control or added cost in the abstract. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, Dodd-Frank’s “only if” and “in accordance with Barnett Bank” language calls for a practical, evidence-based showing that the law prevents or significantly interferes with a national bank power, not a categorical rule that any compelled financial term is preempted. Barnett itself distinguishes meaningful impairment from incidental conditions, so I cannot accept Alito’s proposed per se approach without collapsing Congress’s chosen standard into broader obstacle preemption. The narrow, legitimacy-protecting path is to reject the Second Circuit’s categorical reasoning and remand for application of the correct Barnett/§ 25b test to the law’s real-world effects.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that a compelled escrow-interest payment “controls” a term of the escrow relationship and can affect uniformity, but § 25b(b)(1)(B)’s text preempts “only if” the state law, applied “in accordance with” Barnett Bank, “prevents or significantly interferes” with a national bank power—language that demands a demonstrable, material impairment rather than a categorical rule that any state-set financial term is preempted. Barnett’s own distinction between laws that effectively forbid or meaningfully curtail a federal power and those that impose incidental conditions keeps McCulloch from becoming a freewheeling obstacle-preemption license here, especially after Congress’s deliberate narrowing in Dodd-Frank. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the Second Circuit’s reasoning appears too per se; the proper application is case-specific and record-based, and on this record the escrow-interest mandate looks more like an added condition/cost than a negation of the bank’s lending or servicing power. Because Alito’s approach would read “significantly” out of § 25b and broaden preemption beyond the statute’s original public meaning, I remain with the Petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s point that § 25b’s “only if” language cautions against treating any added cost or administrative adjustment as “significant interference,” and that Barnett Bank requires a practical inquiry rather than slogans about uniformity. But the New York mandate is not merely an incremental compliance cost; it compels a pricing term on a federally authorized escrow function and thus “controls” the exercise of a national-bank power in the Barnett/McCulloch sense, because it dictates how the bank must structure compensation for holding escrowed funds. Even on an evidence-based approach, a state-imposed, non-negotiable interest payment on escrow balances materially alters the economics of mortgage servicing and effectively rewrites the bank-customer bargain, which is the kind of direct state control Barnett described as “hamper[ing]” federal power. Dodd-Frank’s codification narrows preemption doctrine, but it does not require courts to treat compelled financial terms as presumptively insignificant simply because the bank can still make loans.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press that an escrow-interest mandate “directly controls” a financial term and can erode national-bank uniformity, but § 25b’s “only if” and “in accordance with Barnett Bank” language (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress) makes that control relevant only insofar as it amounts to a demonstrated, meaningful impairment of the federally conferred power—not a categorical trigger for preemption. Barnett’s “control” language cannot be severed from its functional touchstone—whether the state law effectively forbids or materially curtails the activity—and on this record the requirement looks like a traditional, borrower-protective incident of escrow administration rather than a practical denial of the power to service mortgages. Justice Kavanaugh’s institutional suggestion to vacate and remand for an evidence-grounded application of Barnett/§ 25b reinforces that we should avoid converting Dodd-Frank’s cabined standard into a per se rule that any state-set pricing term is “significant interference.” Under my pragmatic approach, absent concrete proof that this modest interest requirement substantially restricts access to credit or disables escrow servicing, I cannot treat it as preempted simply because it affects profitability or uniformity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press that an escrow-interest mandate is not just a disclosure rule—it dictates a financial term and thus “touches” a core aspect of escrow administration, invoking McCulloch’s concern with state “control.” But § 25b(b)(1)(B) preempts “only if” the state law, applied “in accordance with” Barnett Bank, “prevents or significantly interferes,” which—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize—cannot be collapsed into a per se rule that any state-set term equals significant interference. Barnett’s own formulation is functional and context-sensitive, distinguishing meaningful impairment from incidental burdens; on this record, the asserted uniformity and cost effects are plausible but not shown to rise to the level of preventing or materially curtailing the federally authorized power. Because Alito’s reading risks reviving the broader obstacle-style preemption Dodd-Frank curtailed, I would reject the categorical approach and require a concrete showing of substantial interference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to emphasize Barnett’s language about state laws that “control” or “hamper” national-bank powers, and an escrow-interest mandate does set a financial term. But § 25b(b)(1)(B)’s text—preempted “only if” the state law “prevents or significantly interferes,” applied “in accordance with” Barnett—requires a materially impairing effect, not a categorical rule that any state-set term is preempted; otherwise we erase Congress’s limiting words. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, the Second Circuit’s approach risks converting Barnett into per se preemption for any added cost or reduced uniformity, which is hard to square with Dodd-Frank’s codification and narrowing. McCulloch supplies the general anti-control principle, but it cannot override § 25b’s demanded showing of significant interference on this record, so my vote remains for the Petitioner (at least to reject the categorical reasoning and require a context-specific application).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press that an escrow-interest mandate dictates a financial term and can matter for national uniformity, and Barnett/McCulloch do not treat that as irrelevant. But § 25b(b)(1)(B) expressly cabins preemption to laws that, in accordance with Barnett Bank, actually “prevent or significantly interfere” with the bank’s power; that language resists converting “control” into a per se rule whenever a State affects pricing or terms. As the Chief Justice explains, the Second Circuit’s reasoning risks collapsing the statutory standard into categorical preemption based on cost/control, whereas Congress in Dodd-Frank demanded a practical, evidence-grounded inquiry into material impairment. Institutionally, the sound course is to vacate/remand (or narrowly reverse) to require that Barnett/§ 25b standard be applied with concrete proof of significant interference, not assumptions about uniformity or profit impact.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that a compelled escrow-interest payment “directly controls” a pricing/administration term and thus could “hamper” a federally authorized banking function under Barnett Bank and McCulloch. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 25b(b)(1)(B) preempts “only if” the state law, applied “in accordance with” Barnett, actually “prevents or significantly interferes” with the bank’s exercise of its powers; that text resists converting any state-imposed term or added cost into categorical preemption. McCulloch’s anti-control principle helps identify when state law disables federal functions, yet Dodd-Frank’s codification demands a practical showing of material impairment akin to effective forbiddance, not an assumption that uniformity or profit impacts alone are “significant interference.” I would therefore reject the Second Circuit’s categorical reasoning and favor a narrow disposition (vacatur/remand) requiring an evidence-grounded application of the Barnett/§ 25b standard.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that an escrow-interest mandate “directly controls” a pricing/administration term and could erode national-bank uniformity, but § 25b(b)(1)(B) makes preemption turn “only if” the state rule in fact “prevents or significantly interferes,” as applied “in accordance with” Barnett Bank—language that rejects a categorical control-equals-preemption rule. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Dodd-Frank was designed to require a practical, evidence-grounded inquiry into meaningful impairment, not an assumption that any compelled financial term is inherently disqualifying. McCulloch’s anti-burden principle still matters, but it operates through Congress’s codified Barnett standard here; without a concrete showing that this interest requirement materially curtails the bank’s ability to offer or service mortgages (as opposed to adding cost or reducing profit), I don’t see “significant interference” on this record. Justice Kavanaugh’s suggestion of a narrow vacatur/remand to correct the Second Circuit’s categorical reasoning fits that procedural posture and keeps our holding tethered to § 25b’s demanding threshold.

John Roberts.reasoning: Dodd-Frank directs that state consumer financial laws are preempted only if, “in accordance with” Barnett Bank, they “prevent[] or significantly interfere[] with” a national bank’s powers. 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B). A generally applicable escrow-interest requirement regulates the terms of a mortgage escrow relationship but does not forbid escrow accounts or materially curtail the bank’s ability to make or service mortgages; under Barnett Bank, added costs or administrative adjustments alone are not necessarily “significant interference” absent a showing that the state law meaningfully impairs the federally authorized power. Given Congress’s choice to codify Barnett and to cabin broader OCC-style preemption, a narrower ruling rejecting categorical “cost-equals-preemption” reasoning better respects precedent, federalism, and institutional legitimacy while leaving room for case-specific proof of substantial impairment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text Congress enacted in 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B) preempts a “State consumer financial law” only if, “in accordance with” Barnett Bank, it “prevents or significantly interferes with” a national bank’s exercise of its powers; a mere increase in costs or an incidental operational requirement is not the same as prevention or significant interference. New York’s escrow-interest mandate (N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-601) regulates the terms of an escrow relationship ancillary to mortgage lending and does not bar or materially impair the bank’s federally granted lending power under the National Bank Act. Under the Supremacy Clause and McCulloch, preemption is warranted when state law frustrates execution of a federal power, but § 25b’s codified Barnett standard requires a demonstrable, significant impairment, which has not been shown here. Because the Second Circuit’s approach risks converting “significantly interferes” into a broader obstacle-preemption rule untethered to § 25b’s text, I would reverse and hold the law not preempted on this record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 25b(b)(1)(B) codifies Barnett Bank’s rule that a state consumer financial law is preempted when it "prevents or significantly interferes with" a national bank’s exercise of its powers, and New York’s escrow-interest mandate materially intrudes on the federally authorized pricing and administration of mortgage escrow accounts. Under Barnett Bank v. Nelson, 517 U.S. 25 (1996), and the broader structural principle of McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819), States may not impose regulatory requirements that meaningfully burden the exercise of national banking powers even if those requirements take the form of generally applicable consumer-protection measures. Requiring national banks to pay interest on escrow balances functions as a compelled financial term of the mortgage/escrow relationship, with practical consequences for uniformity and cost that amount to significant interference rather than a mere incidental effect. Dodd-Frank did not replace Barnett with a more restrictive rule; it directed courts to apply that standard, which here supports preemption given the law’s direct control over a core aspect of escrow operations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Dodd-Frank instructs that state consumer financial laws are preempted “only if” they “prevent[] or significantly interfere[] with” national bank powers, and that determination must be made “in accordance with” Barnett Bank. 12 U.S.C. § 25b(b)(1)(B). A requirement to pay modest interest on borrowers’ escrow balances functions as a traditional consumer-protection and fairness measure governing the terms of an escrow relationship, not a prohibition on mortgage lending or escrow administration, and added compliance costs alone do not establish the kind of meaningful impairment Barnett Bank contemplated. Because New York’s law regulates the incidental consequences of a banking activity rather than barring or materially obstructing the activity itself, the Second Circuit’s approach risks reviving the expansive preemption Congress sought to cabin in § 25b and should be rejected in favor of a more context-sensitive Barnett inquiry.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 25b(b)(1)(B) codifies Barnett Bank’s requirement that a state consumer financial law is preempted “only if” it “prevents or significantly interferes with” a national bank’s exercise of its powers, demanding a context-sensitive conflict-preemption inquiry rather than a per se rule. A state requirement to pay interest on mortgage escrow balances looks like a generally applicable consumer-protection/contract term that increases cost but does not, without more, bar or materially impair the bank’s ability to make mortgage loans or to maintain escrow accounts; under Barnett Bank, added expense and administrative adjustment alone are not necessarily “significant interference.” Dodd-Frank’s framework also cautions against expansive, bank-favoring preemption and requires coherent, workable line-drawing that preserves space for traditional state regulation absent a demonstrated practical impairment of a federal banking power. On this record as described, the Second Circuit’s “any control equals significant interference” approach is too blunt and inconsistent with § 25b(b)(1)(B)’s “only if” limitation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 25b(b)(1)(B) says a “State consumer financial law” is preempted “only if” it “prevents or significantly interferes with” a national bank’s exercise of its powers, codifying Barnett Bank’s narrower, conflict-based approach rather than a freewheeling “any added cost/control” theory of preemption. On the face of the New York escrow-interest requirement, the law regulates the incidents of an escrow relationship without forbidding mortgage lending or escrow collection, so it is not self-evident that it “prevents” or “significantly interferes” with any federally conferred power under Barnett Bank. Dodd-Frank’s textual insistence on that specific standard, and its framework for careful, case-by-case preemption determinations, counsels against converting preemption into a per se rule whenever state law affects pricing or administration. And to the extent the bank relies on OCC regulations or broad assertions of burden untethered to § 25b’s “only if” condition, separation-of-powers principles and skepticism of agency-driven preemption reinforce enforcing the statute’s plain limits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 25b(b)(1)(B) requires a practical, context-sensitive application of Barnett Bank’s “prevents or significantly interferes with” standard, not a categorical rule that any added cost or administrative requirement is preempted. Under Barnett Bank, state laws are displaced when they effectively “forbid” or meaningfully “impair” the exercise of a national bank power, 517 U.S. at 33–34, and Dodd-Frank’s codification signals Congress’s intent to anchor preemption in that bounded inquiry rather than broad field preemption. A requirement to pay interest on escrow balances regulates a term of the bank-customer relationship and, without more, looks like a generally applicable consumer-financial rule that changes pricing and accounting but does not prevent national banks from making mortgage loans or maintaining escrow accounts. On this record, I would vacate and remand for application of the correct Barnett/§ 25b framework to determine whether the interference is truly “significant” in practice, rather than presumed from compliance costs alone.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 25b(b)(1)(B) preempts a “State consumer financial law” only if it “prevents or significantly interferes with” a national bank’s powers, and it directs courts to apply that standard “in accordance with” Barnett Bank, 517 U.S. 25 (1996). A state requirement to pay a modest, fixed rate of interest on escrow balances regulates the terms of an ancillary account relationship and does not, on its face, forbid or materially curtail the federally authorized power to make mortgage loans or to use escrow accounts, unlike the state prohibition at issue in Barnett Bank. Consistent with McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316 (1819), and Barnett Bank’s focus on laws that “control” or effectively negate a federal power, an added cost or operational condition—without a showing of meaningful impairment—falls short of “significant interference.” Dodd-Frank’s codification and cabining of NBA preemption in § 25b counsels against treating any state-imposed pricing term as per se preempted, and the Second Circuit’s approach appears insufficiently context-sensitive to that statutory command.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 25b(b)(1)(B) provides that a state consumer financial law is preempted “only if” it “prevents or significantly interferes with” a national bank’s powers, codifying the context-sensitive Barnett Bank standard rather than a per se rule that any state “control” or added cost triggers preemption. Requiring interest on escrow balances operates as a generally applicable consumer-protection/contract rule governing funds the bank holds for the borrower, and without a concrete showing that it meaningfully impairs the bank’s exercise of mortgage-lending or escrow administration powers, it does not rise to the level of “significant interference.” Dodd-Frank’s framework in § 25b also reflects Congress’s intent to cabin expansive NBA preemption and to insist on a real, evidence-based conflict inquiry, not categorical displacement of state protections. On this record as framed, I would reverse and require the lower court to apply Barnett Bank’s practical, fact-specific inquiry rather than treating the escrow-interest mandate as automatically preempted.
